entries.lesson_core_move: Apply the continuous-time Fourier transform linearity property to compute the spectrum of a weighted sum of signals by carrying the same weights onto their transform-domain terms.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Linearity
sections.learning_goal: State the CTFT linearity rule and show how coefficients pass unchanged from the time-domain sum to the frequency-domain sum.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the lesson is symbolic and uses only known Fourier pairs.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate any images; the tutorial should stay entirely in symbolic transform notation.

question_policy.practice_question_model: No practice questions for the tutorial section.
distractor_plan: No distractors because this section has no questions.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Teach that if $x_1(t)$ has spectrum $X_1(j\omega)$ and $x_2(t)$ has spectrum $X_2(j\omega)$, then $a x_1(t)+b x_2(t)$ has spectrum $aX_1(j\omega)+bX_2(j\omega)$.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Begin with one known pair and a scalar multiple so the learner sees the coefficient carry straight through the transform.
paragraph_plan: Open with why linearity matters: it lets the learner reuse known Fourier pairs instead of recomputing integrals.
Show the base case of a single scaled signal and its matching scaled spectrum.
Extend to the sum of two known signals with unit weights so the learner sees term-by-term addition.
Extend to a weighted sum and stress that each weight stays attached to its own spectrum term.
Close with the general pattern for any finite weighted sum, because the later examples will only vary coefficients and the number of terms.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the exposition short, explicit, and formula-driven so the learner is ready to apply the rule mechanically in the worked examples.

sections.section_title: Transforming a Scaled Signal
sections.learning_goal: Carry a single scalar through a known CTFT pair.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the example is a purely symbolic coefficient-carrying transform.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate any images for the worked example or its questions.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic CTFT choices with exactly one correct spectrum expression.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given $x(t) \leftrightarrow X(j\omega)$, compute the CTFT of $-5x(t)$.
distractor_plan: Omit the scalar multiplier entirely.
Apply the scalar to the time-domain signal but not the spectrum.
Flip the sign of the coefficient.
Confuse coefficient-carrying with time scaling.
Return the original transform pair unchanged.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Given that $x(t)$ has CTFT $X(j\omega)$, find the CTFT of $3x(t)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that multiplying a signal by a constant multiplies its transform by the same constant.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This is the simplest concrete application of linearity: one known pair and one scalar factor.
solution_step_plan: State the known transform pair for $x(t)$.
Apply linearity to the scalar multiple $3x(t)$.
Attach the same factor to the spectrum to get $3X(j\omega)$.
Write the final transform pair cleanly in one line.
practice_variation_axes: Use a different scalar, including a negative coefficient.
Swap in a different known pair from the earlier transform-pair lesson.
Change the signal name while keeping the same coefficient-carrying structure.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep this example scalar-only and unambiguous; later practice should vary the coefficient but not introduce any new CTFT property.

sections.section_title: Transforming a Sum of Two Signals
sections.learning_goal: Transform a two-term sum by adding the two known spectra term by term.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the example is a symbolic two-term sum with known transform pairs.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate any images for this section.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic CTFT choices with exactly one correct sum of spectra.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given $u(t) \leftrightarrow U(j\omega)$ and $v(t) \leftrightarrow V(j\omega)$, compute the CTFT of $u(t)+v(t)$.
distractor_plan: Omit one of the two spectra.
Add the time-domain signals but leave the spectrum expression incomplete.
Turn the sum into a product.
Invent an extra coefficient that is not present.
Confuse the spectrum names and swap them with unrelated notation.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: If $x_1(t) \leftrightarrow X_1(j\omega)$ and $x_2(t) \leftrightarrow X_2(j\omega)$, find the CTFT of $x_1(t)+x_2(t)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the spectrum of a sum is the sum of the spectra when each term already has a known transform pair.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This adds a second known pair but keeps the weights equal to 1 so the learner can focus on the structure of the sum.
solution_step_plan: Identify the CTFT pair for each summand.
Apply linearity to each term separately.
Combine the two spectra with a plus sign.
State the final CTFT of the sum in pair notation.
practice_variation_axes: Change which two known pairs are being added.
Keep the structure symbolic but vary the signal names.
Allow a simple subtraction only if the coefficient structure is still obvious.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep this section at the two-term, unit-weight level so the learner practices additive structure before coefficients get involved.

sections.section_title: Transforming a Weighted Sum of Two Signals
sections.learning_goal: Carry distinct weights through a two-term sum without changing the transform rule.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the example is a symbolic weighted sum of two known pairs.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate any images for this section.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic CTFT choices with exactly one correct weighted sum of spectra.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given $u(t) \leftrightarrow U(j\omega)$ and $v(t) \leftrightarrow V(j\omega)$, compute the CTFT of $2u(t)-3v(t)$.
distractor_plan: Apply both weights to the same spectrum term.
Drop the minus sign on the second term.
Add the coefficients before transforming.
Omit one of the weighted spectrum terms.
Treat the coefficients as if they were time-scaling factors.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: If $x_1(t) \leftrightarrow X_1(j\omega)$ and $x_2(t) \leftrightarrow X_2(j\omega)$, find the CTFT of $2x_1(t)-3x_2(t)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that each coefficient remains attached to its own spectrum term, including a negative coefficient.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This is the first fully weighted two-term sum, so the learner must preserve both coefficients instead of relying on unit weights.
solution_step_plan: Identify the known pair for each signal.
Apply linearity to the first weighted term.
Apply linearity to the second weighted term and keep the negative sign.
Combine the transformed terms into one spectrum expression.
practice_variation_axes: Use different integer coefficients, including one negative coefficient.
Swap in a different pair of known transform pairs.
Change the order of the terms while keeping the same weighted-sum structure.

sections.handoff_notes: This section should make coefficient preservation feel routine; the only job is to keep each weight attached to the right spectrum term.

sections.section_title: Transforming a Multi-Term Weighted Sum
sections.learning_goal: Extend linearity to a three-term or longer weighted sum by transforming each term separately and summing the results.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the example is a symbolic multi-term weighted sum.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate any images for this section.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic CTFT choices with exactly one correct multi-term weighted spectrum.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given $p(t) \leftrightarrow P(j\omega)$, $q(t) \leftrightarrow Q(j\omega)$, and $r(t) \leftrightarrow R(j\omega)$, compute the CTFT of $3p(t)+q(t)-2r(t)$.
distractor_plan: Drop one of the three terms.
Combine all coefficients into a single factor.
Attach the coefficients to the wrong spectrum terms.
Ignore the negative sign on the last term.
Treat the three-term sum as if only the first two terms were transformed.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: If $x_1(t) \leftrightarrow X_1(j\omega)$, $x_2(t) \leftrightarrow X_2(j\omega)$, and $x_3(t) \leftrightarrow X_3(j\omega)$, find the CTFT of $x_1(t)-2x_2(t)+4x_3(t)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that linearity applies term by term to every piece of a multi-term sum, with each coefficient preserved.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This adds a third term and a mixed-sign coefficient pattern so the learner must keep the sum organized across more than two pieces.
solution_step_plan: Rewrite the input as a sum of three separately transformable terms.
Transform the first term.
Transform the second term with its negative coefficient.
Transform the third term with its positive coefficient.
Collect the transformed terms into one final spectrum.
practice_variation_axes: Change the number of terms while keeping the same linearity rule.
Vary the coefficient pattern, including mixed signs.
Swap in different known transform pairs from the earlier Fourier-pair lesson.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the final step explicitly term-by-term and do not introduce any other CTFT property; the only skill here is carrying coefficients across a finite sum.

entries.lesson_core_move: Convert a time shift x(t - t0) into the Fourier-domain factor e^(-j omega t0) X(j omega) so known transform pairs can be reused in transform-property calculations.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Time Shifting
sections.learning_goal: State the Fourier transform time-shift rule and the delay/advance sign convention so the learner can reuse known pairs immediately.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; the step is fully symbolic.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Teach the delay/advance rule $x(t-t_0) \leftrightarrow e^{-j\omega t_0}X(j\omega)$ and the matching advance rule so a shifted signal can be transformed from a known pair.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Start with a known pair $x(t) \leftrightarrow X(j\omega)$ and a simple delayed copy $x(t-t_0)$ with no extra scaling or other properties.
paragraph_plan: Open by framing the lesson as a way to reuse known Fourier pairs when the time signal is shifted.
State the delay property and show how the shift becomes the multiplicative factor $e^{-j\omega t_0}$.
State the advance version $x(t+t_0) \leftrightarrow e^{+j\omega t_0}X(j\omega)$ and tie the sign to the sign inside the parentheses.
Close with one compact symbolic substitution that shows the property in use and hands off to the worked examples.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the introduction compact, avoid magnitude-phase commentary, and stop after establishing the shift/sign rule.

sections.section_title: Transforming a Delayed Signal from a Known Pair
sections.learning_goal: Apply the delay rule to a simple known pair with a numeric shift.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; the step is fully symbolic.

question_policy.practice_question_model: If $x(t) \leftrightarrow X(j\omega)$, what is the Fourier transform of $x(t-3)$?
distractor_plan: Use the wrong exponential sign, such as $e^{+j3\omega}$.
Drop the shift factor and return only $X(j\omega)$.
Confuse the time shift with a frequency shift.
Apply the factor to the wrong quantity instead of the spectrum.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Given $x(t) \leftrightarrow X(j\omega)$, find the Fourier transform of $x(t-2)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show the learner how to identify the known pair, read the delay amount, and attach the factor $e^{-j2\omega}$ to the original spectrum.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This is the first concrete application after the tutorial: one known pair, one numeric delay, and no extra algebra.
solution_step_plan: Name the base pair $x(t) \leftrightarrow X(j\omega)$.
Recognize $x(t-2)$ as a delay of 2.
Multiply the known spectrum by $e^{-j2\omega}$.
State the final transformed pair in one line.
practice_variation_axes: Change the known pair while keeping a single delay.
Change the delay amount without changing the method.
Switch between a delay and an advance so the sign convention still matters.

sections.handoff_notes: Use a single known pair and one numeric delay; keep both follow-up questions symbolic and focused on the shift factor.

sections.section_title: Transforming an Advanced Signal from a Known Pair
sections.learning_goal: Recognize a shifted causal signal as a delayed version of a known pair and attach the correct Fourier-domain factor.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; the step is fully symbolic.

question_policy.practice_question_model: If $e^{-2t}u(t) \leftrightarrow \frac{1}{2+j\omega}$, what is the Fourier transform of $e^{-2(t-4)}u(t-4)$?
distractor_plan: Omit the delay factor entirely.
Use the wrong sign in the exponential factor.
Change the denominator as if the shift altered the base pair itself.
Treat the signal as a frequency shift instead of a time shift.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Given $e^{-t}u(t) \leftrightarrow \frac{1}{1+j\omega}$, find the Fourier transform of $e^{-(t-3)}u(t-3)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show how to recognize the shifted causal exponential, reuse the known pair, and carry the delay factor through without redoing the transform integral.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The signal is more structured than a bare delayed copy, so the learner must recognize the shifted base pair before applying the same time-shift rule.
solution_step_plan: Identify the unshifted pair $e^{-t}u(t) \leftrightarrow \frac{1}{1+j\omega}$.
Rewrite the signal mentally as a delay of that base signal.
Attach the factor $e^{-j3\omega}$ to the base spectrum.
Write the final spectrum with the original denominator unchanged.
practice_variation_axes: Change the exponential rate in the base pair.
Change the shift amount while keeping the same causal shape.
Swap the base pair to another known 9.2 transform pair.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the challenge in recognition, not algebra: the example should be a shifted known pair that still resolves to one factor times one base spectrum.

sections.section_title: Choosing the Sign in the Time-Shift Factor
sections.learning_goal: Choose the correct positive or negative exponent when the time shift is written as an advance or a delay.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; the step is fully symbolic.

question_policy.practice_question_model: If $x(t) \leftrightarrow X(j\omega)$, what factor multiplies $X(j\omega)$ for $x(t+4)$?
distractor_plan: Use $e^{-j4\omega}$ instead of $e^{+j4\omega}$.
Drop the sign and write a generic shift factor with no direction.
Confuse the advance with a delay and reverse the exponent sign.
Apply the factor to the wrong base spectrum.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Given $x(t) \leftrightarrow X(j\omega)$, find the Fourier transform of $x(t+4)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Force the learner to read the plus sign in the time argument as an advance and therefore use the factor $e^{+j4\omega}$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The only new wrinkle is the direction of the shift: the learner must avoid defaulting to the delay sign.
solution_step_plan: Translate $x(t+4)$ into an advance of 4.
Match an advance to the positive exponent $e^{+j4\omega}$.
Attach that factor to $X(j\omega)$ and state the result.
practice_variation_axes: Use different positive and negative shifts.
Write the shift inside a longer expression so the sign is easier to miss.
Keep the same base pair but vary the amount of advance or delay.

sections.handoff_notes: Make the sign choice explicit in the prompt and in the solution path so the later questions can test advance-versus-delay recognition cleanly.

sections.section_title: Applying Time Shifting to a Shifted Sum of Known Pairs
sections.learning_goal: Combine linearity with time shifting to transform a weighted sum of shifted known pairs.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; the step is fully symbolic.

question_policy.practice_question_model: If $g(t)=3x(t-1)-2x(t+2)$ and $x(t) \leftrightarrow X(j\omega)$, what is $G(j\omega)$?
distractor_plan: Apply one shift factor to the whole sum instead of splitting the terms.
Forget one coefficient or one shifted term.
Use the wrong sign on one of the shift factors.
Combine the terms before transforming and lose the linearity structure.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Given $x(t) \leftrightarrow X(j\omega)$, find the Fourier transform of $3x(t-1)-2x(t+2)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the learner should split the weighted sum term by term, transform each shifted copy separately, and then recombine the pieces.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This adds the linearity layer: the learner must transform multiple shifted terms before combining them into one spectrum.
solution_step_plan: Separate the sum into individual weighted terms.
Transform $3x(t-1)$ as $3e^{-j\omega}X(j\omega)$.
Transform $-2x(t+2)$ as $-2e^{+j2\omega}X(j\omega)$.
Combine the two transformed terms into one expression.
practice_variation_axes: Change the number of shifted terms.
Mix delays and advances in the same sum.
Change the coefficients while keeping the same base pair.

sections.handoff_notes: The writer should transform each term separately and only then combine; later questions can vary the number of terms and the mix of delays and advances.

entries.lesson_title: Magnitude and Phase Effects of Time Shifting
entries.lesson_core_move: Determine how a time shift leaves the Fourier-transform magnitude unchanged while adding the linear phase term -omega t0 to the spectrum.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Magnitude and Phase Effects of Time Shifting
sections.learning_goal: Show that a time shift preserves Fourier magnitude and adds only a linear phase term.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image required; the property is expressed entirely with symbolic Fourier-transform notation.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image for this lesson.

question_policy.practice_question_model: not-applicable

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Show that $x(t-t_0)$ becomes $e^{-j\omega t_0}X(j\omega)$ and that $|e^{-j\omega t_0}|=1$, so the magnitude spectrum is unchanged while the phase gains $-\omega t_0$.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Start with a known pair $x(t)\leftrightarrow X(j\omega)$ and a single delay $t_0>0$, then separate the magnitude and phase of the shifted spectrum.
paragraph_plan: Recall the time-shift property from the previous lesson and narrow the focus to what changes in magnitude and phase.
Write $x(t-t_0)\leftrightarrow e^{-j\omega t_0}X(j\omega)$ and point out that the extra factor has unit magnitude.
Show why the magnitude spectrum stays the same.
Show the phase becomes the original phase minus $\omega t_0$ and interpret the slope.
Note that an advance simply flips the sign of $t_0$; later examples will use both signs.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the explanation tightly symbolic and use the previous time-shifting notation as the bridge; the writer should not re-derive the Fourier integral or introduce plots.

sections.section_title: Magnitude Spectrum of a Time-Shifted Signal
sections.learning_goal: Show that delaying a signal does not change the magnitude spectrum.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image required; the magnitude comparison is handled symbolically.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image for this lesson.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic choices; select the magnitude spectrum that remains unchanged after the time shift.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given $y(t)=x(t-t_0)$ and $X(j\omega)$, choose the expression for $|Y(j\omega)|$.
distractor_plan: Use the shifted spectrum itself instead of its magnitude.
Multiply the magnitude by the complex exponential time-shift factor.
Introduce an unrelated frequency shift or amplitude scaling.
Negate or invert the magnitude expression.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: If $x(t)\leftrightarrow X(j\omega)$ and $y(t)=x(t-2)$, what is $|Y(j\omega)|$?
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Write $Y(j\omega)=e^{-j2\omega}X(j\omega)$ and conclude that $|Y(j\omega)|=|X(j\omega)|$ because $|e^{-j2\omega}|=1$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This is the first concrete delay case and it asks only for magnitude, so the student must separate magnitude from the phase factor.
solution_step_plan: Write the transformed spectrum using the shift property.
Take the magnitude of both sides.
Use $|e^{-j2\omega}|=1$.
Conclude that the magnitude spectrum is unchanged.
practice_variation_axes: Change the delay value.
Use an advance instead of a delay while still asking for magnitude.
Give the spectrum in symbolic form and ask for the unchanged magnitude.
Mix in a nontrivial original magnitude expression such as a sinc or rational form.

sections.handoff_notes: Generate two symbolic multiple-choice questions that keep the same magnitude and vary only the delay amount or the original magnitude expression.

sections.section_title: Phase Change from a Time Delay
sections.learning_goal: Combine the original phase spectrum with the delay-induced linear term $-\omega t_0$.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image required; the phase change is handled entirely with symbolic expressions.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image for this lesson.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic choices; select the phase expression obtained after a delay.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given $\angle X(j\omega)=\omega/2$ and $y(t)=x(t-3)$, choose the correct expression for $\angle Y(j\omega)$.
distractor_plan: Flip the sign of the linear phase term.
Keep only the original phase and ignore the shift.
Use the magnitude spectrum in place of the phase.
Substitute the wrong delay amount into the slope.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: If $x(t)\leftrightarrow X(j\omega)$ and $\angle X(j\omega)=\omega/2$, what is $\angle Y(j\omega)$ for $y(t)=x(t-3)$?
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Carry the original phase forward and subtract $3\omega$ from it to get the new phase spectrum.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The example now tracks phase instead of magnitude and keeps the original phase term, so the student must add the delay-induced slope rather than replace the whole spectrum.
solution_step_plan: Write the shift factor for $y(t)=x(t-3)$.
Extract its phase contribution $-3\omega$.
Add that to the given phase $\omega/2$.
State the result and confirm that the magnitude is unchanged.
practice_variation_axes: Change the delay value.
Use a different original phase expression.
Ask for the slope of the new phase instead of the full expression.
Present a near-miss sign choice so the student must distinguish delay from advance.

sections.handoff_notes: Generate two symbolic multiple-choice questions: one direct delay case and one near-miss sign variation that still requires the student to add $-\omega t_0$ to the original phase.

sections.section_title: Phase Change from a Time Advance
sections.learning_goal: Apply the advance-induced linear phase term $+\omega t_0$ without changing the magnitude spectrum.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image required; the advance case is handled symbolically.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image for this lesson.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic choices; select the phase expression obtained after an advance.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given $\angle X(j\omega)=\omega/2$ and $y(t)=x(t+3)$, choose the correct expression for $\angle Y(j\omega)$.
distractor_plan: Use the delay sign instead of the advance sign.
Omit the shift term and keep only the original phase.
Treat the magnitude as if it changed.
Use the wrong advance amount in the phase slope.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: If $x(t)\leftrightarrow X(j\omega)$ and $\angle X(j\omega)=\omega/2$, what is $\angle Y(j\omega)$ for $y(t)=x(t+3)$?
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Recognize that advancing the signal adds $+3\omega$ to the original phase.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This is the mirror image of the delay example, so the only new idea is that the sign of the linear phase term flips when the signal is advanced instead of delayed.
solution_step_plan: Write the shifted spectrum using $x(t+3)$.
Extract the phase contribution $+3\omega$.
Add it to the original phase $\omega/2$.
State the result and note that the magnitude still does not change.
practice_variation_axes: Swap delay for advance.
Change the advance amount.
Keep the same base phase but vary the original slope.
Ask the student to identify advance versus delay from the sign of the phase slope.

sections.handoff_notes: Generate two symbolic multiple-choice questions that force the student to reverse the sign compared with the delay case and still keep the magnitude unchanged.

sections.section_title: Identifying a Time Shift from Linear Phase
sections.learning_goal: Infer the delay or advance from a linear phase term of the form $\pm\omega t_0$.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image required; infer the shift directly from symbolic phase terms.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image for this lesson.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic choices; choose the time shift implied by the linear phase term.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given a linear phase of $-4\omega$, identify the corresponding time shift and direction.
distractor_plan: Flip the sign and confuse delay with advance.
Divide the slope incorrectly when solving for $t_0$.
Treat a constant phase offset as the time shift.
Claim the magnitude changes when the phase slope changes.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: If $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)e^{-j4\omega}$, what time shift does $y(t)$ represent relative to $x(t)$?
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Match the phase slope to $-\omega t_0$ and conclude that the signal is delayed by $4$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The reasoning now runs backward: instead of predicting the phase from a known shift, the student reads the phase slope and identifies the shift direction and size.
solution_step_plan: Identify the linear phase term.
Match the coefficient of $\omega$ to $-t_0$ or $+t_0$.
Solve for the time shift and state delay or advance.
Confirm that the magnitude is unchanged.
practice_variation_axes: Use a negative slope of a different size.
Use a positive slope so the student must identify an advance.
Include an extra constant phase offset and ask the student to ignore it when reading the shift.
Present multiple equivalent expressions for the same delay.

sections.handoff_notes: Generate two symbolic multiple-choice questions: one from a negative linear phase slope and one from a positive slope, both asking for the inferred time shift.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Time Scaling
sections.learning_goal: Teach the student to apply the CTFT time-scaling rule to a known pair by replacing $t$ with $at$, scaling frequency by $1/a$, and carrying the $1/|a|$ magnitude factor.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Show the student that compressing or expanding time rescales the CTFT on the frequency axis and multiplies the spectrum by $1/|a|$.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Start with $x(t) \leftrightarrow X(j\omega)$ and the concrete case $x(2t)$ so the student sees the simplest compression before generalizing.
paragraph_plan: Restate a known Fourier transform pair and introduce the question of what happens when the time variable is multiplied by a scale factor.
